module.title: Special Talents & Skills: 'Good at' & 'Bad at'
module.objective: Communicate personal talents, special skills, and proficiencies using the 'good at' and 'bad at' patterns followed by gerunds.

content.summary: In this reading mission, you will read a short text about friends and their special talents. You will learn how to find the main idea, scan for important details, and understand sentences with good at and bad at. You will also see how people talk about activities such as drawing, singing, playing music, and organizing.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Use subject + am/is/are + good at or bad at + verb-ing. For example: She is good at drawing. They are bad at remembering names.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Words for talents and skills, including talent, skill, brilliant, hopeless, drawing, organizing, remembering, practice, and improve.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: First, skim the text to find the main topic. Then, scan the text for names, activities, and skill words such as good at, bad at, and brilliant at.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of a short A1 passage about special talents and skills.
Identify key details about what people are good at and bad at.
Recognize good at and bad at followed by a verb ending in -ing.
Use names, activities, and skill words to answer reading questions.

contextWarmup.prompt: Which sentence tells us about a person's special skill?
options: She is good at drawing animals.
contextWarmup.explanation: The first sentence is correct because it uses the pattern she is good at + drawing. After at, use an activity ending in -ing.

rules: Use good at or bad at to describe how well someone does an activity.
After at, use a noun or a verb ending in -ing: good at music, good at singing.
Look for the person's name first, then find the activity after good at or bad at.
Words such as brilliant, excellent, quite good, and hopeless give extra information about skill level.

commonTrap.explanation: Do not use the base verb after at. The word at is followed by a noun or an -ing form.
commonTrap.wrong: He is good at play the guitar.
commonTrap.correct: He is good at playing the guitar.

content.context: Class 7 is preparing for a school talent afternoon. Three friends talk about their skills and work together.
content.text: On Friday, Class 7 has a talent afternoon. Mia and her friends talk about their special skills. Mia is good at drawing animals. She brings three pictures of cats and birds to school. Her friend Leo is brilliant at playing the guitar. He practices in his room every day and can play two songs for the class. Anna is quite good at organizing activities. She makes a simple plan for the afternoon and writes everyone's name on a list. But Anna is bad at singing, so she does not want to sing alone. Leo is not very good at remembering words, and Mia is hopeless at dancing. They laugh, but they help each other. Mia makes a poster, Anna organizes the chairs, and Leo plays music. At the end, their teacher says, "Everyone has a special talent. Practice helps us improve."

highlights.note: Use good at + verb-ing to describe a skill.
Brilliant means very good at something.
Use bad at + verb-ing to describe an activity that is difficult for someone.
Practice can help people become better at a skill.

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Talents at the School Show

content.summary: In this listening mission, two students talk about their talents for a school talent show. Listen for the phrase "good at" or "bad at" followed by an activity ending in -ing. Also listen for words that describe ability, such as brilliant, excellent, terrible, and hopeless.
learningObjectives: Identify activities that people are good at and bad at.
Understand "good at + -ing" and "bad at + -ing" in a short conversation.
Listen for key details about talents, plans, and extracurricular activities.

keyPhrases.note: Use "good at" before an activity ending in -ing to describe a skill.
Use "bad at" before an activity ending in -ing to describe something difficult for you.
Use "brilliant at" to say that someone has a very strong skill.
Use "terrible at" to describe an activity that is very difficult for you.
Use this phrase when people decide to work or perform together.
Use this phrase when people prepare for an activity as a team.

sections.title: Audio Dialogue: Planning for the Talent Show

content.context: Sarah and David are talking in the school cafeteria about extracurricular activities, the school talent show, and their special talents.
content.audioPrompt: Listen carefully to the following dialogue between two students.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: Hi David! Are you joining the school talent show this year?
lines.translation: Hai David! Apakah kamu akan ikut pertunjukan bakat sekolah tahun ini?

lines.speaker: David
lines.text: I'm not sure. I'm quite good at playing the guitar, but I'm terrible at performing in front of people.
lines.translation: Aku tidak yakin. Aku cukup pandai bermain gitar, tapi aku sangat buruk tampil di depan orang banyak.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: Really? You should try! I'm hopeless at playing instruments, but I'm brilliant at dancing.
lines.translation: Benarkah? Kamu harus mencoba! Aku sangat buruk memainkan alat musik, tapi aku sangat pandai menari.

lines.speaker: David
lines.text: That's great! Are you good at singing too?
lines.translation: Itu bagus! Apakah kamu juga pandai menyanyi?

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: Not really. I'm bad at singing, but my brother is excellent at it. He's in a band.
lines.translation: Tidak juga. Aku buruk dalam bernyanyi, tapi kakakku sangat pandai dalam hal itu. Dia ada di sebuah band.

lines.speaker: David
lines.text: Cool! Maybe we can form a group. You dance, I play guitar, and your brother sings!
lines.translation: Keren! Mungkin kita bisa membentuk grup. Kamu menari, aku bermain gitar, dan kakakmu menyanyi!

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: That's a brilliant idea! Let's practice together this weekend.
lines.translation: Itu ide yang cemerlang! Ayo berlatih bersama akhir pekan ini.

lines.speaker: David
lines.text: Perfect! I'm good at organizing practice schedules. I'll send you a message later.
lines.translation: Sempurna! Aku pandai mengatur jadwal latihan. Aku akan mengirim pesan kepadamu nanti.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: My Skills and Talents

content.summary: Use good at or bad at to write about skills, talents, and activities. After at, use a verb with -ing, such as swimming, drawing, or playing. You can also use a noun, such as math or languages.

blueprintItems.title: Add Good at or Bad at
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + am/is/are + good at / bad at

blueprintItems.title: Add an Activity
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + am/is/are + good at / bad at + verb-ing

blueprintItems.title: Add a Skill Level
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + am/is/are + brilliant / great / quite good / not very good / terrible at + verb-ing
blueprintItems.example: He is brilliant at playing chess.

mechanicsRules.rule: Start every sentence with a capital letter and end it with a full stop.
mechanicsRules.why: English sentences need a capital letter at the start and a full stop at the end.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use am with I, is with he, she, and it, and are with you, we, and they.
mechanicsRules.why: The verb be must match the subject.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use a verb ending in -ing after at.
mechanicsRules.badExample: My brother is good at cook.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: My brother is good at cooking.
mechanicsRules.why: After at, use the -ing form of an activity verb.

mechanicsRules.rule: You can use a noun after at when you write about a school subject or skill.
mechanicsRules.why: Math is a noun, so it can come after at without -ing.

sampleSentences.en: My sister is great at dancing.
sampleSentences.id: My sister is great at dancing.

sampleSentences.en: We are quite good at math.
sampleSentences.id: We are quite good at math.

sampleSentences.en: They are not very good at speaking English.
sampleSentences.id: They are not very good at speaking English.

mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Use a capital I, use a verb ending in -ing after at, and add a full stop.

mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Use is with she and use playing after at.

mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Use are with friends and use singing after at.

mechanicsChallenges.faultySentence: we are quite good at draw
mechanicsChallenges.targetSentence: We are quite good at drawing.
mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Use drawing after at and end the sentence with a full stop.

practicumQuestions.prompt: Write two complete sentences about your skills. Use good at + verb-ing in both sentences.

practicumQuestions.criteria: Use he, she, or a name correctly. Use is correctly. Include good at in one sentence and bad at in one sentence. Use -ing after at.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: My brother is good at playing football. He is bad at cooking.

practicumQuestions.criteria: Write at least three complete sentences. Use am, is, or are correctly. Include good at or bad at. Use at least one skill level word and correct -ing forms.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: My friend Ana is brilliant at dancing. I am quite good at drawing. We are good at speaking English. My brother is terrible at singing.

content.summary: Talk about your talents with clear sentences such as "I am good at drawing" and "I am bad at cooking." After "good at" and "bad at," use a verb ending in -ing.
content.audioGuidance: Speak slowly and clearly. Stress the important words, especially the skill word: "good at DRA-wing" and "bad at COOK-ing." Use a falling voice for statements. Use a rising voice for yes or no questions, such as "Are you good at singing?"

pillars.name: Clear Sentence Pattern
pillars.target: Use good at and bad at with an -ing verb
pillars.explanation: Say "I am good at playing football" or "I am bad at cooking." Do not say "good at cook."

pillars.name: Strong Skill Words
pillars.target: Stress the main skill or activity
pillars.explanation: Make the activity easy to hear. For example, say "I am good at DANC-ing" and "I am bad at SWIM-ming."

pillars.name: Question Intonation
pillars.target: Use rising intonation in yes or no questions
pillars.explanation: Let your voice rise at the end of a question: "Are you good at drawing?"

pillars.name: Confident Delivery
pillars.target: Share one strength and one skill to improve
pillars.explanation: Speak with a friendly voice. It is okay to be bad at something. You can add, "I need more practice."

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: The stress moves from the first syllable in "PHOtograph" to the second syllable in "phoTOGraphy."
The stress moves from "MUsic" to the middle syllable in "muSIcian."

drills.focus: The phrase good at and the -ing ending
drills.hint: Link "good at" smoothly. Make the first syllable of "drawing" strong.
Say the final sound in "bad" before "at": "bad-at."

drills.targetText: Are you good at playing basketball?
drills.focus: Rising intonation in a yes or no question
drills.hint: Let your voice rise on "basketball" because this is a question.
Say the final /d/ in "need" and the first syllable of "PRACTice" strongly.
